title: Large-Scale Plasma Proteomics and Genetic Integration Uncover Novel Biological Pathways in Male Pattern Baldness
abstract: Male pattern baldness (MPB) is a highly prevalent condition with a complex, poorly understood molecular basis that limits therapeutic innovation. This study aimed to bridge the gap between statistical genetic associations and biological function by identifying and prioritizing causal proteins and pathways involved in MPB. Using data from 24,069 men in the UK Biobank, we performed a proteome-wide association study of 2911 plasma proteins with self-reported MPB severity via multivariable ordinal logistic regression, adjusting for age, Body Mass Index (BMI), ethnicity, lifestyle, socioeconomic factors, and testosterone levels. Significant proteins underwent pathway enrichment analysis. Genetic integration included MAGMA for gene-level aggregation and tissue prioritization, transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) with GTEx models, conditional fine-mapping, and validation in an independent scalp biopsy transcriptomics dataset (GSE90594). Druggability and pleiotropy were evaluated using databases and phenome-wide association studies. Forty-seven proteins were significantly associated with MPB severity, enriched in pathways involving epidermis development, hair cycle regulation, and cell adhesion. Multi-omic integration prioritized five independent candidate genes: CD38, FGF5, TACSTD2, DPEP1, and PLB1. Transcriptomic validation confirmed differential expression in balding scalp for CD38 (upregulated) and TACSTD2, PLB1 (downregulated). CD38 was identified as druggable with low pleiotropic risks. This study elucidates the molecular architecture of MPB, revealing novel biological pathways beyond canonical androgen signaling. By prioritizing promising non-hormonal targets like CD38, our findings provide a robust, evidence-based framework to guide the development of future therapeutic interventions for this common condition.

title: Vitamin D-Related Signaling and Epigenetic Regulation: Evidence from Experimental, Observational, and Interventional Studies
abstract: The active vitamin D metabolite, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol [1,25(OH)2D], exerts its biological effects through binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR), a ligand-activated transcription factor regulating the expression of genes involved in calcium and phosphate homeostasis, immune modulation, and cell proliferation and differentiation. In addition to direct transcriptional regulation, 1,25(OH)2D signaling also involves epigenetic mechanisms. A total of 90 studies were included in this narrative review, comprising experimental studies (n = 45), observational studies (n = 17), population-based studies (n = 8), interventional studies (n = 15), and mixed-design studies (n = 5). Experimental studies in cell cultures and animal models demonstrate that 1,25(OH)2D may affect several major epigenetic regulatory pathways, including chromatin remodeling, DNA methylation, histone modifications, and the expression of non-coding RNAs, particularly microRNAs. Preclinical evidence suggests that the epigenetic actions of 1,25(OH)2D are involved in metabolic regulation, immune responses, bone development, fibrotic processes, carcinogenesis, ageing, and fetal programming. However, evidence from observational studies and randomized controlled trials remains limited and inconclusive. Some studies have reported alterations in miRNA expression, methylation of selected loci, and epigenetic age markers. The clinical relevance of 1,25(OH)2D–mediated epigenetic regulation has not yet been fully established. The interpretation of available findings is limited by substantial heterogeneity in study populations, exposure and intervention protocols, environmental factors, interindividual variability in response to vitamin D supplementation associated with genetic polymorphisms and methylation status, and the restricted range of analyzed cell types. This subject requires randomized controlled trials integrating molecular endpoints with clinically relevant outcomes.

title: Healthy aging, living longer, or living forever
abstract: INTRODUCTION Aging is considered a natural and unavoidable side effect of life though it can vary widely between species and individuals.[1] From time immemorial, the mighty king, queens, saints, and ordinary human beings, tried unusual methods to become immortal. Mythologies are full of such stories, and many of us still believe in them despite lacking scientific evidence. Nevertheless, the quest for immortality or living longer is still on. The present article is written to sum up in a few pages about aging, longevity, and immortality. LONGEVITY OF ORGANISMS Today there is only one animal that may be considered immortal: some species of Jellyfish. These transparent small animals float around in the sea and can revert to their earlier stages of development. Research shows that these creatures have double the number of genes that repair and protect DNA, thus protecting the telomere. The genetic mutation may also increase the longevity of an organism. This fact has already been proved in yeast cells, microscopic roundworms, and fruit flies. The single gene mutation has also been responsible for longevity in mice, the animal genetically closer to human beings. Yeast cell has played a critical role in revealing the molecular genetics of fundamental processes such as cell cycle, protein folding, and intracellular trafficking. Drosophila melanogaster showed that longevity increases due to overexpression of genes involved in stress response.[2] LONGEVITY IN HUMAN BEINGS One of our oldest research questions is how long human beings can live.[3] The answer to this question is debatable. Some feel we have already reached the limit, whereas others say there is no limit.[4] United Nations estimates that 573,000 persons over 100 were alive in 2020. This is 20 times the number 50 years ago. The current longevity record is held by French woman Jan Calment who passed away at the age of 122 years. The life expectancy in Sweden and Japan increased by 3 months per year since 1840. Currently, Japanese women have the highest life expectancy of 87 years.[4] Life expectancy in India was 70.15 years in 2020, whereas at the time of independence in 1947, it was only 32 years. However, some researchers feel that life expectancy increases due to reduced infant mortality. SCIENTISTS AND THEIR PATHBREAKING RESEARCH Leonard Hayflick experimented back in 1961, placing human fetal cells in a Petri dish, allowing them to divide. The cells split 50–60 times and then stopped. It reinforces the idea that death is inevitable.[5] Ray Kurzweil; “2045: The Year Man become immortal” was on Time magazine’s front page in 2011. Ray Kurzweil is a renowned futurist who believes that by 2045 we might become immortal. His concept was that we could transfer the data from our brains to a computer, leave our bodies, and work as machines. In brief, man and machine can become one. Kruzweil’s other concept uses nanotechnology and artificial intelligence to replace suboptimal biology to make humans live forever. There is some chance that his concepts may become a reality in times to come—Arthur Levinson, a scientist and a businessman. He has been a pioneer in producing insulin and hepatitis B vaccines through pathbreaking recombinant technology. He was involved with multiple genetically engineered drugs and later became chairman of Genentech Inc, South San Francisco, California, United States. He is also on board of Apple Inc, Cupertino, California, United States. He boosted genetic research, which may pave the way for finding more about the genetic aspect of aging. Craig Venter—a scientist credited for rapidly sequencing the human genome and creating life in the lab. His passion for genetic research is unparallel in the world. He was sure that understanding chronic diseases and aging is the secret to understanding the human genome. GENETICS AND AGING The focus of research on aging has shifted to the genetics of aging and identifying genes responsible for longevity. The search for longevity genes in humans is still on. Telomeres are DNA—protein structures that form protective caps at the end of the eukaryotic chromosome.[6] They contribute to safeguard chromosome degradation and are responsible for maintaining genomic integrity. Telomere length is highly variable based on the age and sex of the individual and inversely proportional to chronological age. Accelerated telomere loss has been associated with many chronic diseases of aging. Premature aging is seen in early life through increased oxidative stress and DNA damage to the telomeric end.[7] Genomic instability includes somatic mutation, inappropriate DNA methylation, and increased histone modification. DNA methylation correlates with chronological age precisely, thus providing aging clocks.[6] Mitochondrial dysfunction is also evident with growing age. RECENT PATHBREAKING RESEARCH MAY REVOLUTIONIZE THE UNDERSTANDING OF AGING In a comprehensive review in a high-ranking journal, “Cell” in 2013, Lopez-Otin et al.[8] identified nine tentative hallmarks of aging with particular reference to mammalian aging. These hallmarks are telomere attrition, genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, stem cell exhaustion, deregulated nutrient sensing, cellular senescence, and altered intercellular communication. Even today, the primary research focuses on these nine molecular aging sensors. Yang et al.,[9] in January 2023, published an article in the same journal titled “Loss of epigenetic information as a cause of mammalian aging.” The highlights of this article are as follows: (a) it is the loss of epigenetic information rather than DNA mutation that may be responsible for aging and (b) by epigenetic manipulation, aging can be moved forward or backward, which means that aging could be accelerated or reversed. So far, the experiments have been conducted on mice with spectacular results. INFLAMMATION AND IMMUNE PARAMETERS AND AGING Acute inflammation is necessary to fight invading infections or tissue insult and help in healing. It is chronic inflammation that leads to aging and reduces the life span. There is evidence that some age-related diseases such as ischemic heart disease, diabetes, sarcopenia, and malignancy are associated with the elevation of circulating inflammatory mediators. It is known today that the immune system activity diminishes with age. It becomes slower to respond, the vaccines may not work, and autoimmune disorders may develop. There may be increased chances of developing cancer because the body’s ability to detect and correct cell defects is compromised. In animal studies regarding immune parameters, better immune functionality is seen in a group of mice that survived longer.[10] RESURRECTION AFTER DEATH Alcor life extension foundation is all about freezing the body after death in the hope that it can be resurrected later when technology advances. This facility is available in Scottsdale, Arizona, USA. More than 1000 persons have registered for cryogenic freezing after death. The cost of freezing the body is about 200,000 dollars (one crore and seventy lakh in Indian rupees), and then, there is recurrent expenditure every year. Some people take this in a very optimistic way; their concept is that if we take it as an experiment with a control, control means 100% death, but the study group may not be 100% failure. Not everyone is amused by the explanation, some call them nuts. PROMISING REMEDIES THAT MAY DELAY AGING Diet and nutrition The Okinawa diet is critical to the long life of people living in the Ryukyu islands of Japan. There are more than 500 people who are more than 100 years. The diet of these islanders contains 30% of green and yellow vegetables, fish, and a small quantity of pork, soy, and rice. Staple food for them is purple color sweet potato. Bitter melon is another widespread plant that is very popular and can regulate blood sugar. Overall, this diet is of low caloric value and low in fat. There is a saying in the islands that “Eat enough to fill up only 80% of your belly.” Eating right and less could be the “mantra” for living longer. The Mediterranean diet is considered one of the best to prevent age-related diseases. It prevents cardiovascular disease (CVD), regulated blood sugar levels, and increases life span. This diet includes fruits, vegetables, nuts, fish and sea foods, whole grains, beans, olive oil, herbs, and spices. On the other hand, some foods such as hot dogs, bacon, cheeseburger, soft drinks, and packaged and refined food items decrease life expectancy. Cruciferous vegetables, green salads, nuts, seeds, berries, pomegranates, beans, mushrooms, onion, garlic, and tomatoes are the best food to increase longevity. These foods are said to be preventing cancer too. Refined sugar in any form may lead to unhealthy aging. Wine in moderation may act as an antioxidant and promote healthy aging. There is another school of thought: some feel that by using “recombinant technology,” we may create a superfood to help reduce the incidence of age-related diseases and increase longevity. Healthy environments, particularly those experienced during early life, are hypothesized to affect longevity. A recent cross-taxa meta-analysis found that depending upon the circumstance, average longevity may be increased or decreased by early-life dietary restriction. Longevity is around 8% higher under early-life dietary restriction than under a standard diet. Early-life dietary restriction may also generate a variance in longevity.[11] Physical activity Humans have known that physical activity (PA) promotes health and longevity. Over the last few decades, studies have shown that 150 min/week walk of moderate intensity or 75 min/week walk of vigorous intensity reduces the relative risk of all-cause mortality by 50%. PA reduces the risk of hypertension, CVD, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer’s, and many cancers. As a result, physical exercise significantly increases quality-adjusted life years and reduces disability-adjusted life years.[12] Regular PA prevents weight gain, maintains normal blood pressure, lowers low-density lipoproteins and triglycerides levels, and increases high-density lipoproteins (HDLs). It also reduces systemic inflammation, decreases stress levels, and stimulates the production of neurotransmitters and neurotrophins that maintain neurons and ameliorate mood.[13] The rough estimate is that 1 h of exercise adds 2 h to our life. Moderate levels of life-prolonged exercise have played a unique role in our evolutionary biology and extended our life span. Regular “Yoga” also helps in disease-free aging and increases longevity. Helen Hayes says, “Resting is Rusting,” and we think she is right. However, exercises do not prevent old age diseases such as cataracts, loss of hearing, and prostate enlargement. Slower resting heart rate Studies have indicated that a low resting heart rate is associated with health and longevity, and conversely, a high resting heart is associated with disease and adverse events.[14] Recent animal research has suggested that heart rate lowering with sinus node inhibition is associated with increased lifespan.[14] It is mentioned in “Ayurveda,” an ancient text, that Rishi (Sages) were able to lower their heart rate with the help of Yoga and lived longer. Even today, heart rate-lowering drugs such as beta-blockers help decrease the mortality of cardiac patients. Among the animals, “Whales’ may have heart rates as low as 02 per minute and may live up to 200 years. Even a tortoise with a slow heart rate (10–25) may live for 100 years. Animals with very high heart rates, such as rats and birds, have a shorter life span. The rats have heart rates of 300–500 beats per minute and live for 2–4 years. The fact is that most of the smaller animals have higher heart rates and shorter lives. The development of personal digital devices such as mobile phones, fitness trackers, and eHealth applications has made heart rate information readily available to the public and clinicians.[13] Scientists have also discovered that the carriers of the longevity gene BPIFB4 live longer and have fewer cardiac disorders. Focus is now on implanting this gene in humans through an adenovirus vector and reducing atherosclerosis in coronary vessels. DRUGS AND OTHER THERAPIES Metformin Metformin is a safe and efficient glucose management drug in patients with diabetes. In recent years more attention has been paid to the possibility of using metformin as an anti-aging drug.[10] Clinical trial evidence suggests that metformin can reduce the risk of many age-related diseases and conditions, including cardiometabolic disorders, neurodegeneration, and chronic inflammation. Metformin also holds promise as a drug that could be repurposed for chemoprevention or adjuvant therapy for certain types of cancer. Moreover, metformin induces autophagy by activation of AMPK and can, thus, be potentially used to promote health span by hormesis-like mechanisms.[13] Rapamycin Rapamycin inhibits RNA translation and protein synthesis and promotes autophagy by suppressing the activity of mTOR complex 1 and is used clinically to prevent rejection of transplanted organs. The impact of Rapamycin on aging with particular attention to health span is tested in domestic dogs and nonhuman primates with promising results.[6] Antioxidants Many studies are showing the beneficial effects of antioxidants on aging. However, it could not be conclusively proved by animal experiments.[9] Stem cells, gene editing, and aging Scientist Bob Hariri was the one who wanted to use stem cells as an alternate treatment for age-related diseases. He was more interested in placental stem cells. His motto was to turn “Stem cells into medicine.” Stem cells injected directly into damaged organs generated stronger and newer cells and helped in healing. Initial enthusiasm about stem cell treatment is over as the treatment did not bring consistent results. However, the researchers have not given it up, and possibly one day, it may help in treating age-related diseases and, thus, increasing longevity. Harvard genetic professor George Church announced in 2015 that he could reverse the aging process in the next 5–6 years. George was a key player in developing the simple and effective Gene-editing system—clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and probably wanted to use it to reverse aging. However, after fierce ethical debate, CRISPR was banned for human gene editing. Chinese scientist Jiankui, without ethical clearance, used CRISPR to alter embryos in a woman who later had twin baby girls. The whole world was shocked as he had changed the human DNA forever. Apart from using the gene-editing tool “CRISPR” for increasing longevity, another field of research is genetically modifying hearts and lungs, and other organs in pigs that can later be used for human transplantation. HEALTHY AGING OR LIVING LONGER I have always wondered, “Why do we want to live longer?.” The answer could be that, at the moment, there is enough evidence that animals and humans are genetically programmed “to try to live longer.” Though, if there is a choice between healthy aging or living longer with many diseases, most of us will prefer healthy aging and not unhealthy longevity. However, the preference would be longevity if given the option to live longer and be healthy. For a nation, a younger and more productive population is preferable to an older population because the aging population is less effective and consumes more resources. CAN HUMAN BEINGS LIVE FOREVER OR, IN OTHER WORDS, BECOME IMMORTAL Many scientists, biologists, and physicians agree that life expectancy for human beings will keep increasing until it reaches its limit of 120–150 years, but living forever may not be possible shortly. As of now, the process of aging appears inevitable. However, we may be able to slow the aging process with ideal nutrition, good exercise, good health care, good genes, and a bit of luck. What means do we have to live longer and live healthy at the moment: Good physical exercise Eat healthily, change to white meat and oily fish, and do not overeat Avoid refined sugar Good physical exercise No smoking Drink in moderation Keep your weight in check Healthy sleep (6–8 h) Blood pressure in a healthy range Blood glucose in a healthy range Non-HDL cholesterol in a healthy range Have a good gene Living forever or reversing aging may be called science fiction, but we cannot say with certainty that it will remain science fiction. With the brain-computer interface, genetic editing by a crisper understanding of epigenetics, stem cell technology, and the production of genetically compatible organs for human beings from animals, we may at least dream of immortality as a possibility. But if this possibility becomes a reality, “How will we sustain such a large population? Some scientists say that the population could be controlled by castrating everybody. title: Decoding Cardiac Aging: Integrative Genetic, Cellular, and Molecular Insights Through a Data-Driven Perspective
abstract: Background: Cardiac ageing is driven by interlocking defects in mitochondrial quality control, telomere–senescence biology, endothelial–microvascular homeostasis, extracellular-matrix remodelling, and proteostasis, culminating in diastolic dysfunction, arrhythmia substrate, and impaired reserve in older adults. Mechanistic mapping and translational appraisal are needed to prioritize tractable therapeutic nodes. Objective: To synthesize genetic, cellular, and molecular mechanisms of cardiac ageing; distinguish physiological from pathological trajectories; and evaluate translational strategies spanning lifestyle, pharmacology, and targeted molecular approaches. Methods: We conducted a prespecified narrative review (searches to 10 November 2025) across MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL, plus trial registries and reference lists. Dual screening and domain-appropriate appraisal were applied. Evidence was thematically organized across mitochondria/oxidative stress, telomere–senescence, endothelial dysfunction, fibroblast activation, proteostasis/autophagy, epigenetics, and nodal pathways (mTOR, AMPK, FOXO, SIRT1/PGC-1α, Wnt/β-catenin, TGF-β, NF-κB). Results: Of 5,633 records, 4,419 were screened; 698 full texts were assessed; 186 studies were included (human observational n=74; human interventional n=12; animal n=82; in-vitro n=18). Consistent signals implicate diminished AMPK–SIRT1/PGC-1α and FOXO activity, heightened TGF-β/Wnt profibrotic drive, and chronic NF-κB–mediated inflammaging. Exercise robustly engages mitochondrial and autophagic programs; mTOR modulation and senescence-targeted strategies show preclinical efficacy but require cautious human translation. Conclusion: Cardiac ageing reflects convergent failures in energy, repair, and matrix homeostasis. Near-term impact is most likely from exercise-centred programs, with selective evaluation of mTOR and senescence-directed therapies in rigorously phenotyped older adults. Harmonized endpoints and multi-omic biomarkers are priorities for trials

title: BIOINFORMÁTICA NA IDENTIFICAÇÃO DO FENÓTIPO SECRETOR ASSOCIADO À SENESCÊNCIA (SASP) NO PROCESSO DO ENVELHECIMENTO CUTÂNEO.
abstract: This paper presents a literature review on the use of bioinformatics tools for the identification of molecular biomarkers related to cellular rejuvenation. The aim is to analyze how bioinformatics integrated with omics methodologies (with emphasis on proteomics) can contribute to the discovery of relevant biomarkers. Descriptors related to biomarkers, bioinformatics, senescence and rejuvenation were used from databases such as NCBI, PubMed, Google Scholar and Scielo. Skin aging results from interactions between genetic,environmental and epigenetic factors, leading to structural and functional changes in the skin. Changes in DNA methylation, histones and chromatin contribute to cellular senescence and tissue degradation, impacting skin homeostasis. The identification of biomarkers, such as SASP, is essential to understand these processes and develop effective therapeutic strategies. Bioinformatics has emerged as a fundamental tool in the analysis and interpretation of omics data, enabling the integration of large volumes of genomic, transcriptomic and proteomic information. These approaches allow the discovery of new therapeutic targets and strategies to delay cellular aging. This approach favors the development of personalized interventions, enhancing the prevention and treatment of signs of skin aging and promoting healthy longevity.

title: EMERGING SCIENCE AT THE INTERSECTION OF NUTRITION AND AGING
abstract: Abstract With the population shifting towards older age, identifying new strategies to promote healthful aging is of paramount importance. Nutritional interventions can delay or prevent the onset of age-related disease and disability. The objective of this symposium is to disseminate novel findings from multidisciplinary research conducted at the USDA Human Nutrition Research Center on Aging at Tufts University that describe: (1) The inter-play between the diet and the gut microbiome with respect to reducing macular degeneration, the leading cause of vision loss in older age. (2) The molecular basis of a gene-diet interaction that influences age-related obesity discovered using an integrative –omics approach in three population-based cohorts. (3) A new function for a known micronutrient in maintaining mobility in older age, identified in a population-based prospective study of older adults. Collectively this symposium provides mechanistic insight into potentially new nutritional strategies to promote healthy and active aging.
